summaryEn: A Taiwanese maker of power transformers and switchgear that has become a direct beneficiary of the AI power crunch — winning transformer orders for America's Stargate datacentre project and holding a backlog booked through 2028. Explosive earnings growth, an extraordinary 54% return on equity, and a valuation to match.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; heavy-electrical framing — the Stargate/AI-datacentre orders, NT$30bn backlog to 2028, rising gross margin and ~54% ROE credited, but the sharply negative recent monthly revenue, ~27.9x book valuation and leveraged small equity base stated plainly; no cause asserted for the revenue dip because none could be verified; sector/nameZh/listedYear fixed, foundedYear left null)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Fortune Electric (華城電機, TWSE: 1519) makes **power transformers, switchgear and distribution equipment** — the unglamorous hardware that stands between a power station and everything that uses electricity. It is the first **heavy electrical equipment** company in this collection, and it occupies a position that has become unexpectedly strategic: **the world cannot build AI datacentres faster than it can build the grid equipment to power them**, and transformers have become one of the hardest bottlenecks to clear.

The order book shows it. Fortune Electric won the **first-phase power transformer order — around NT$2bn — for the Texas "Stargate" AI project**, and its **AI-datacentre-related orders now exceed NT$10bn**. In the fourth quarter of 2024 alone it added **NT$12bn of new orders, NT$6bn of them from AI datacentres**. Its **total backlog exceeds NT$30bn and is booked through 2028**, and it has been **expanding capacity 30–40% a year** to meet it. Brokers project 2026 revenue approaching **NT$31bn**.

The financial transformation has been dramatic. Annual EPS ran **NT$3.21 (FY2022) → 9.87 (FY2023) → 15.13 (FY2024) → 14.26 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 EPS of NT$3.29, up about 10% year-on-year**, while **gross margin climbed from 35.9% to 43.6%** — pricing power in a shortage. The dividend followed: **NT$0.4 (2017) → 2.5 (2022) → 6.0 → 9.0 → 11.0 (2025)**. Return on equity is an extraordinary **53.6%**.

Two things keep this honest. First, **monthly revenue has just turned sharply negative — down 9.3% in May and 25.8% in June 2026** — and no published explanation could be verified; with a multi-year backlog, monthly figures reflect **shipment timing rather than demand**, but the deterioration is real and worth watching. Second, the stock trades at roughly **50× earnings and 27.9× book**, on a balance sheet where **equity is only NT$8.5bn against NT$29.9bn of assets** (a 71.7% debt ratio). The honest read: **a genuine bottleneck supplier riding one of the strongest capital-spending waves in decades — priced as though nothing can go wrong.**

Fortune Electric belongs to an old and normally uneventful industry. It builds **transformers** — the machines that step voltage up for transmission and down for use — along with **switchgear, distribution panels and turnkey electrical engineering**. For most of its history this was a stable domestic business serving Taiwan's utility, industrial and construction customers, and the company **listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in April 1997**.

What changed was not the company but the world's demand for electricity. Two forces arrived together. **Grid replacement**: transformer fleets installed decades ago across the United States and Europe reached the end of their lives at the same time, while renewable generation required entirely new interconnections. **AI datacentres**: hyperscale computing campuses need power at a scale that dwarfs conventional facilities, and each one requires large power transformers that take **years, not months, to build**. Global transformer capacity had not been expanded for a generation, and lead times stretched dramatically.

For a competent transformer maker with spare engineering capability, this was transformative. Fortune Electric pushed into **export markets, above all the United States**, and won a landmark contract: the **first-phase power transformer order for the Texas "Stargate" AI project**, worth around **NT$2bn**. AI-datacentre-related orders passed **NT$10bn**, backlog swelled beyond **NT$30bn stretching to 2028**, and the company began **expanding capacity by 30–40% a year**. A company whose earnings per share were **NT$3.21 in 2022** was earning **NT$15.13 by 2024** — not because it invented anything, but because the world suddenly needed far more of what it had always made.

- **1997 (16 Apr)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1519)**, making transformers, distribution panels and electrical equipment, plus turnkey engineering.
- **2000s–2010s** — A steady domestic heavy-electrical supplier; dividends of NT$0.3–1.3 a share.
- **2021–2022** — Global grid replacement and renewable interconnection demand begins to tighten transformer supply; FY2022 EPS **NT$3.21**, dividend NT$2.5.
- **2023** — Earnings triple: **EPS NT$9.87**; dividend NT$6.0.
- **2024** — **EPS NT$15.13**; dividend NT$9.0. **Q4 adds NT$12bn of orders, NT$6bn from AI datacentres**; capacity expansion of 30–40% a year begins.
- **2025** — **EPS NT$14.26**, dividend **NT$11.0**; wins the **first-phase transformer order (~NT$2bn) for the Texas Stargate AI project**; AI-datacentre orders exceed **NT$10bn**; **backlog above NT$30bn booked to 2028**.
- **2026** — Gross margin reaches **43.6%** and 2026Q1 EPS **NT$3.29 (+10% YoY)**, but **monthly revenue turns negative (−9.3% May, −25.8% June)**; brokers project full-year revenue near **NT$31bn**.

Fortune Electric's accounts show a company being reshaped by a demand shock — with the leverage that rapid expansion requires.

- **Explosive, then plateauing, earnings.** Annual EPS **NT$3.21 (FY2022) → 9.87 → 15.13 (FY2024) → 14.26 (FY2025)** — a more than fourfold increase in two years, followed by a modest dip. **2026Q1 EPS of NT$3.29** was about 10% ahead of the prior year.
- **Margin expansion, the signature of scarcity.** Gross margin rose from **35.9% (2025Q1) to 43.6% (2026Q1)** and operating margin sits around **21%**. In a genuine shortage, a supplier prices for its scarcity — and this is what that looks like in the accounts.
- **An extraordinary return on a small equity base.** **ROE of 53.6%** is remarkable, but it is partly arithmetic: **equity is only NT$8.46bn** against **NT$29.9bn of assets**, giving a **71.7% debt ratio**. Rapid capacity expansion is being funded with liabilities as well as retained profit, which magnifies returns in good times and risk in bad ones.
- **A dividend that tracked the boom.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$0.4 (2017) → 1.0–1.3 (2019–2021) → 2.5 (2022) → 6.0 (2023) → 9.0 (2024) → 11.0 (2025)** — a 27-fold increase in eight years. At NT$668 the yield is nonetheless only **~1.65%**.
- **A valuation that assumes the boom continues.** Roughly **50× earnings and 27.9× book**. A price-to-book approaching 28 for a heavy-equipment manufacturer is only defensible if the current return on equity persists for many years.

The financing reality: **a company converting a global shortage into exceptional profits, funded partly by leverage, and valued as if the shortage is permanent.**

**Stance: a genuine bottleneck supplier to the AI and grid buildout, with visible multi-year orders and exceptional returns — priced at ~28× book, with monthly revenue already wobbling.**

The bull case:

1. **A verified, multi-year order book.** Backlog **above NT$30bn booked through 2028**, including the **first-phase transformer order for the Texas Stargate AI project (~NT$2bn)** and **over NT$10bn of AI-datacentre-related orders**. Revenue visibility of this length is rare.
2. **Structural scarcity, not a cycle.** Transformer capacity was not expanded for a generation while **grid replacement, renewable interconnection and AI datacentres arrived simultaneously**. Lead times are measured in years, which is why **gross margin has risen from 35.9% to 43.6%**.
3. **Exceptional returns and a rising dividend.** **ROE of 53.6%**, EPS up more than fourfold since FY2022, and dividends up from NT$0.4 to **NT$11.0**.

The counter-arguments:

- **Revenue has just turned sharply negative.** **−9.3% in May and −25.8% in June 2026.** No published explanation could be verified. With a multi-year backlog this most likely reflects **shipment timing**, but it is exactly the kind of signal that a stock priced for perfection cannot absorb.
- **The valuation leaves no room.** Roughly **50× earnings and 27.9× book** for a heavy-equipment maker; a **1.65% yield** provides no support.
- **Leverage on a thin equity base.** A **71.7% debt ratio** with only **NT$8.46bn of equity** funds the 30–40% annual capacity expansion — excellent while orders flow, punishing if they pause.
- **Capacity is the industry's answer.** Every transformer maker in the world is expanding; today's shortage pricing is precisely what invites tomorrow's competition.

A **shortage-economics** thesis: own the bottleneck while it lasts, with clear eyes about what the price already assumes.

Fortune Electric makes money by **manufacturing the equipment that moves and controls electricity**, and increasingly by exporting it:

- **Power transformers (the profit engine).** Large units that step voltage between transmission and distribution levels. They are **engineered to order**, take **many months to build**, require specialised materials and testing, and cannot be substituted or rushed. That is why, when demand exceeds capacity, prices and margins rise sharply — and why the **Texas Stargate order** matters beyond its size: it establishes the company as a qualified supplier to the largest AI infrastructure programmes.
- **Switchgear, distribution panels and equipment.** The lower-voltage apparatus that distributes power inside substations, factories and buildings — steadier, more competitive, and often sold alongside transformers.
- **Turnkey electrical engineering.** Designing and installing complete electrical systems, which pulls through equipment sales and deepens customer relationships.

The economics are **order-book driven**. Revenue is recognised as equipment is built and shipped, so **monthly figures reflect production and delivery schedules rather than current demand** — which is why a company with **NT$30bn of backlog booked to 2028** can nonetheless report a month with revenue down 25%. The levers are **order intake (especially export and AI-datacentre orders), pricing (currently favourable), capacity expansion (30–40% a year), and execution** — building complex equipment to schedule while growing headcount and plant.

The strength is that Fortune Electric sells into a **genuine physical bottleneck** with years of visibility. The vulnerability is equally structural: this is **capital-goods manufacturing**, where a demand plateau leaves the industry with newly expanded capacity, and where today's exceptional margins are a direct function of a shortage that every competitor is racing to relieve.

Heavy electrical equipment is normally a sleepy, cyclical industry. It is currently anything but.

- **A generation of under-investment met three simultaneous demands.** Transformer manufacturing capacity was barely expanded for decades. Then came **replacement of ageing grids** in the US and Europe, **renewable interconnection** requiring entirely new substations, and **AI datacentres** consuming power at unprecedented density. Lead times for large power transformers stretched from months to **years**.
- **Supply cannot respond quickly.** Building transformer capacity requires specialised plant, scarce materials such as grain-oriented electrical steel, and **skilled labour that takes years to train**. This is why the shortage has persisted rather than self-correcting — and why suppliers have enjoyed unusual pricing power.
- **The competitive set.** Global incumbents — **Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Eaton, Schneider** — dominate the largest and highest-voltage equipment, alongside Korean makers (Hyundai Electric, HD Hyundai) that have expanded aggressively into the US. Fortune Electric competes as a **credible, qualified Asian supplier**, winning share because customers need capacity from anyone who can deliver.
- **The obvious risk.** Everyone is expanding. Shortage economics reward incumbents right up until the moment new capacity lands, at which point pricing normalises — a pattern this industry has repeated before.

Fortune Electric's position is **real but not protected by moat**: it is a competent manufacturer benefiting from a genuine, verifiable physical constraint. The industry truth is that **the constraint is temporary by construction** — the entire world is spending to remove it — which is why the length of the backlog matters more than the current margin, and why a valuation of nearly 28× book asks the shortage to outlast the response.

**Strengths**
- **Verified multi-year backlog above NT$30bn booked to 2028**, including the **Texas Stargate first-phase transformer order (~NT$2bn)** and **NT$10bn+ of AI-datacentre orders**.
- **Shortage pricing power**: gross margin up **35.9% → 43.6%**; **ROE 53.6%**; EPS up more than fourfold since FY2022.
- **Rapidly rising dividend** (NT$0.4 in 2017 → **NT$11.0** in 2025); capacity expanding 30–40% a year.

**Weaknesses**
- **Monthly revenue just turned sharply negative** (−9.3% May, −25.8% June 2026), with no verified explanation.
- **Very high valuation**: ~50× earnings, **~27.9× book**, only ~1.65% yield.
- **Leveraged, thin equity base**: 71.7% debt ratio on just NT$8.46bn of equity.

**Opportunities**
- Continued **US grid replacement, renewable interconnection and AI-datacentre** buildout; export share rising.
- Qualification as a supplier to major AI infrastructure programmes opening repeat orders.
- Capacity expansion converting backlog into revenue through 2028.

**Threats**
- **Global capacity additions** by incumbents and Korean rivals relieving the shortage and normalising pricing.
- Execution risk in scaling output 30–40% a year; materials and skilled-labour constraints.
- A pause in datacentre or grid capital spending.

- **The valuation assumes the shortage persists.** At roughly **50× earnings and 27.9× book** with a **1.65% yield**, the price embeds years of exceptional returns. Transformer shortages have historically ended when capacity catches up — and every major producer worldwide is expanding.
- **Recent revenue deterioration.** Monthly revenue fell **9.3% in May and 25.8% in June 2026** year-on-year. No published cause could be verified. A multi-year backlog makes **shipment timing** the most plausible explanation, but investors should treat unexplained revenue declines in a highly-rated stock as a genuine warning rather than dismiss them.
- **Leverage and expansion risk.** A **71.7% debt ratio** on **NT$8.46bn of equity** funds 30–40% annual capacity growth. This amplifies returns now and losses if orders slow before the new capacity is absorbed.
- **Customer and project concentration.** Large orders such as the Stargate contract are lumpy; delays, cancellations or redesigns at a small number of very large projects move results materially.
- **Input and labour constraints.** Grain-oriented electrical steel, specialised components and skilled winding labour are themselves scarce; cost inflation or shortages could squeeze the very margins the boom created.
- **Competitive response.** Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova and expanding Korean makers are adding capacity aimed at the same US demand.

Fortune Electric's outlook depends on a single question: **how long does the transformer shortage last, and how much of it can this company convert into delivered revenue?** The axes to watch:

- **Backlog conversion and monthly revenue.** With **over NT$30bn booked to 2028**, the near-term issue is execution and shipment timing — which makes the **recent monthly declines (−9.3%, −25.8%)** the first thing to monitor, and their reversal the first thing to require.
- **Order intake, especially AI and export.** New orders are the leading indicator: whether **AI-datacentre orders keep building beyond NT$10bn** and whether **export share continues rising**, which would extend visibility past 2028.
- **Margin durability.** Gross margin has climbed to **43.6%** on scarcity. The honest test is whether it holds as global capacity expands — margin, not revenue, is where the shortage ends first.
- **Capacity execution and the balance sheet.** Delivering 30–40% annual expansion on a **71.7% debt ratio** without operational stumbles.

Bottom line: Fortune Electric sells into one of the few **genuine physical bottlenecks** of the AI era — power transformers — with a **verified NT$30bn backlog to 2028**, a landmark **Stargate order**, **gross margin rising to 43.6%** and a **53.6% return on equity**. It is also a **capital-goods manufacturer valued at nearly 28× book**, financed with meaningful leverage, whose **monthly revenue has just fallen sharply for reasons that could not be verified**. Judge it on **order intake, backlog conversion and margin durability** — an outstanding beneficiary of a real shortage, at a price that assumes the shortage outlasts the world's response to it.
